title: Constructivism
summary: Red and black, heavy capitals, and diagonal bars. The poster as a tool of agitation.
lede: The graphic design of Russian and Soviet Constructivism (about 1919–1934): posters, books, and magazines built from red and black on paper, heavy sans-serif capitals, diagonal bars and wedges, and photomontage. The movement also covers sculpture and architecture. This record covers its printed work and treats the other branches as related styles.

era.note: From El Lissitzky’s Red Wedge poster (1919) to the official adoption of Socialist Realism (about 1934). The movement itself dates from about 1915.

lineage.label: Suprematism
lineage.note: Wikipedia states that Constructivism’s geometric abstraction “owed something to the Suprematism of Kazimir Malevich”. Lissitzky made the Red Wedge poster (1919) in Malevich’s UNOVIS group in Vitebsk.

lineage.label: Cubism
lineage.note: Wikidata lists Cubism as an influence (P737). Tate records that Tatlin saw Picasso’s cubist constructions in Paris in 1913 and then made abstract constructions from industrial materials.

lineage.label: Constructivist architecture
lineage.note: The architectural branch of the same movement. This record covers the printed work only.

The Wikipedia infobox lists Bauhaus as indirectly influenced. László Moholy-Nagy took part in the Constructivist International of 1922 and brought constructivist photomontage and typography to the Bauhaus in 1923.
Wikipedia names the book designs of Rodchenko and Lissitzky as a major inspiration for Jan Tschichold. His New Typography is commonly read as a source of the later Swiss style.
The Constructivist International met with De Stijl artists in Germany in 1922, according to Wikipedia.

grammar.text: Red and black printed on the paper color, sometimes with a darker red or a screened tint of black. A third hue is rare. The Stenberg brothers’ film posters are the colorful exception.
Lines of type, bars, and wedges run at steep angles and cross the page. The composition moves toward one point instead of resting on a grid.
Bold sans-serif capitals, often drawn by hand and condensed. Words are stacked, enlarged, turned on the diagonal, or set vertically.
Thick rules, triangular wedges, and circles are active parts of the message, as in Lissitzky’s Red Wedge, not decoration.
Black-and-white photographs are cut out and combined with type and flat shapes, often at extreme angles (Rodchenko, Klutsis, Kulagina).
Solid ink areas from letterpress and lithography. No gradients, shadows, or ornament.

diagnostic: Red and black dominate on a light paper ground.
At least one major element (a line of type, a bar, or a wedge) runs on a diagonal.
Headlines are heavy sans-serif capitals, often stacked or rotated.
Photographs are black and white and cut out, combined with type and flat shapes.
counter: Three or more strong hues, for example a primary triad.
A calm, strictly orthogonal grid with no diagonals.
Serif, script, or ornamental letterforms carry the message.
Gradients, soft shadows, rounded corners, or ornament.
Painted, figurative illustration without geometry (Socialist Realism).

confusions.difference: Bauhaus uses the primary triad, elementary shapes, and often lowercase type. Constructivism is mostly red and black, uses capitals, and depends on diagonals and photomontage. Late Bauhaus print borrowed from Constructivism, so some pieces sit between the two.
The Swiss style is calm and orthogonal, with a strict grid, sentence-case grotesque type, and much white space. Constructivism is loud: diagonals, capitals, and large red fields.
De Stijl allows only horizontal and vertical lines and uses the primaries. Constructivism is built on diagonals and uses red and black.
Art Deco posters (Cassandre) also use diagonals and bold sans-serif type, but add airbrushed gradients, symmetry, metallic color, and ornament.
Soviet posters after about 1934 use painted, figurative illustration. Constructivist posters use geometry, type, and photomontage.

do: Use a paper-colored ground with red and black as the only strong colors.
Set headings in heavy condensed sans-serif capitals. Stack words and use a steep scale contrast.
Put at least one element on a diagonal: a red wedge, a black bar, or a rotated heading or label.
Use large solid red fields for the elements that need the most emphasis, such as the hero, a quote, or the featured offer.
Use thick black bars and rules to direct the eye across the page.
When a page needs images, use black-and-white photographs, cut out and combined with type.
dont: Do not add a third strong hue such as yellow or blue. The page then reads as Bauhaus or De Stijl.
Do not use gradients, soft shadows, rounded corners, or ornament.
Do not rotate body text. Rotate headings, labels, and shapes only.
Do not use Soviet emblems such as the hammer and sickle or the red star as decoration. They carry political meaning.
Do not imitate Cyrillic with Latin letters, for example a reversed R for Я.

fingerprint.note: Positive marker: red is the one strong hue; black, paper, and tints do not count. A second hue points to Pop Art, a triad to Bauhaus or De Stijl. Multicolor posters such as the Stenberg brothers’ fall outside this range. Provisional: set from the specimen, recalibrate with measured references.
Positive marker: red covers real area as bands, wedges, and blocks, not only as an accent line. Provisional: set from the specimen, recalibrate with measured references.
Positive marker: headings, labels, buttons, and slogans are set in capitals. Provisional: set from the specimen, recalibrate with measured references.
Positive marker: headings are heavy block letters. Provisional: set from the specimen, recalibrate with measured references.
Corners are square. Circles appear as shapes.
